sentences.text: Before I show you my solution, let me start with a thirty-second thought experiment.
Imagine these are two satellites. Their predicted orbital paths cross.
Do these two satellites necessarily collide?
Not necessarily. They also have to reach that location at approximately the same time.
That is one of the fundamental ideas behind conjunction assessment.
Now imagine doing this repeatedly, for a changing population of space objects.
We need to know where they will be, when they will be closest, how close they will get, how uncertain that prediction is, and which event deserves attention first.
That is the problem ANTARIKSHA-RAKSHA is designed to support.
Space is becoming increasingly crowded.
The challenge is not simply tracking objects. It is turning changing orbital information into a prioritised, explainable and auditable decision-support workflow.
Think of space as a three-dimensional highway: vehicles travelling at several kilometres per second, with no visible lanes.
ANTARIKSHA-RAKSHA follows seven stages: see, predict, detect, understand, prioritise, explain, and decide.
Data comes in. Physics processes it. Risk prioritises it. AI explains it. A human decides. And the audit trail records what happened.
This is the deployed prototype. It uses public orbital data from CelesTrak, and propagates the objects forward using SGP4.
It screens one hundred and three objects over a seventy-two-hour horizon at a sixty-second step, one thousand and twelve candidate pairs, refreshed automatically every two hours.
The displayed tracks are SGP4-propagated predictions based on the latest available orbital data. This is not continuous sensor-level live telemetry.
For demonstration purposes, the prototype can create controlled geometry derived from ingested orbital data.
This is a controlled simulation for demonstrating the decision workflow. It is not an operational warning.
Here, screening flags CARTOSAT-3 and a Fengyun-1C debris fragment.
TCA means Time of Closest Approach: the predicted moment when the separation between the two objects is smallest.
The miss distance at TCA is twenty metres, at a relative velocity of zero point two kilometres per second.
The prototype calculates a deterministic collision-probability indicator using an analytic encounter-plane model.
This is a simplified analytic collision-probability indicator. It is NOT an operational covariance-based collision probability.
It uses simplified isotropic uncertainty, not authoritative operational covariance, and a twenty-metre hard-body radius.
Monte Carlo is not the production calculation; it is kept only as a test reference.
The event is placed in the Critical tier, and asset criticality raises its priority, for ordering only.
The purpose is not simply to produce a number. It is to help answer: which event deserves attention first?
AI does not calculate the orbit. AI does not calculate TCA, miss distance or collision probability. AI does not command a spacecraft.
AI receives the already-computed backend evidence, and helps turn it into a concise, analyst-oriented explanation.
On this hosted deployment the AI layer is unavailable, so a labelled deterministic template is shown, and the physics and risk assessment remain available.
The operator can approve the assessment, or dismiss it with a reason.
The final decision remains with the human operator, recorded in the audit trail with the account and role that made it.
No command is sent to any spacecraft.
For India, the opportunity is not to replace established orbital tracking or space-situational-awareness capabilities.
It is to build complementary, modular and sovereign software layers that help transform orbital evidence into explainable, prioritised and auditable decision support.
The innovation is in integrating deterministic orbital evidence, transparent risk reasoning, local AI explanation, human governance and auditability into one demonstrable workflow.

These are transparent engineering boundaries: public TLE data; simplified isotropic uncertainty instead of operational covariance; a fixed hard-body radius, weaker for slow co-orbital encounters; no operational validation; and controlled demo scenarios. It is decision support, not spacecraft control.
Next steps: covariance and CDM integration, richer catalogue feeds, higher-fidelity uncertainty propagation, and operational validation.
Space safety is not only about tracking what is in orbit.
It is about understanding what may happen next — and helping the right human make the right decision at the right time.
ANTARIKSHA-RAKSHA.
Physics first. AI second. Human decision last.
